How to Play Codenames: The Spymaster Rules Nobody Teaches You

2026-11-19

How to play Codenames: split into two teams, one spymaster per team gives a single-word clue plus a number, and their teammates guess which cards belong to them. Cover all your agents first and you win. Touch the assassin and you lose on the spot. It plays 4 to 8 people in about 15 minutes and costs $24.97.

If you remember one thing from this page, remember this. Codenames is not really a game about guessing words. It is a game about one person, the spymaster, deciding when to play it safe. Every table learns the rules in two minutes and then loses the same three games the same way. The guessing is easy. The person who can see the answers is the one who quietly gives it away.

I have taught this game more than 30 times, mostly at parties where nobody wanted to read a rulebook. Here is Codenames in the order it actually clicks, plus the spymaster rules most groups never get told.

The Goal and the Board

The table holds 25 codename cards in a 5x5 grid. Underneath them sit secret identities: 9 agents for one team, 8 for the other, 7 innocent bystanders, and 1 assassin.

Blue and red are just team names. The side with 9 cards goes first. The starting team always gets one more card than the other, so the game hands the first move to whoever has more work to do.

Your job is to cover all your agents with your own color. First team to finish wins. The assassin sits hidden in the grid the entire game, wearing the same face as every other card.

Setup in 60 Seconds

You need at least 4 players, split into two teams of similar size. Each team picks one spymaster. Both spymasters sit on the same side of the table, facing their teams.

Shuffle the 25 codenames and lay them out in the 5x5 grid. Then one spymaster slides the key card into the stand between the two spymasters. The key is a map of the grid: blue squares are blue agents, red squares are red agents, pale squares are bystanders, and one black square is the assassin.

Only the spymasters ever see that key. The four lights on the key's edge tell you which team starts, and that team gives the first clue. Everyone else is a field operative.

The Clue: One Word and One Number

On your turn as spymaster, you say one word and one number. The word is your clue. The number tells your team how many of their cards relate to it.

The word must be a single word. No phrases, no extra hints, no gestures, no faces. You also cannot use any codename that is still visible on the table, and that includes other forms of the word. While BREAK is showing, you cannot say break, broken, or breakage either. Once a card gets covered, that word becomes legal again.

Example: two of your words are NUT and BARK. Both grow on trees, so you say "tree, 2". Your team then works out which two words you mean.

Your Turn: Guess, Guess, Guess

Your operatives debate it out loud. You keep a straight face. When they are ready, one of them touches a card, and that touch is the official guess.

Hit one of your own words: you cover it with an agent card, and your team guesses again. Any wrong card ends the turn immediately.

Pay attention to this number: your team may make up to number plus one guesses. Say 3 and they are allowed 4, as long as each guess is right. They must guess at least once, and they can stop early whenever they want. That free extra guess is where a lot of games get won, because it lets a team clean up a word from an earlier clue.

How a Turn Ends

There are four ways, and only one of them is truly bad news.

Your own agent: your team keeps guessing. An innocent bystander: the turn ends, nothing gained and nothing lost. An enemy agent: the turn ends, and worse, that card is now revealed for the other team. You just did their work for them. The assassin: the game ends instantly, and your team loses.

Here is why that last one matters so much. The assassin looks exactly like every other card until someone touches it. One wrong guess in a tight game does not just end your turn. It ends the night, and it ends it with one player feeling like they blew it for everyone.

One endgame rule is worth knowing before you start. You can win on the other team's turn. If they guess your final card by accident, they lose and you win. So never assume a game is over until the last card is covered.

The Spymaster Rules Nobody Teaches You

Here is the key insight. Your clue is not about the words you own. It is about the words you might hit by accident. Before every single clue, find the assassin and the enemy's agents first, then build a clue that steers your team around them.

The second rule is the one I wish someone had taught me on night one. I call it the assassin tax. Every multi-word clue is a bet. Say 4 and you are promising four safe hits in a row. Miss on the second guess and you hand the turn to the other team. Miss on the assassin and the whole game is gone. So before you open your mouth, ask one question: how bad is it if my team is wrong here?

The third rule is free and most spymasters ignore it. Watch the enemy's clue too. If their clue also fits one of your words, their spymaster just told you exactly where your card is. That happens more often than you would think, and it is the quietest way to pick up a free word.

And two numbers you can use that almost nobody knows. You can say 0, which means none of your words relate, and your team still has to guess at least once. You can also say unlimited if your group allows it, which lets them guess as many cards as they want while they keep getting them right. Both are risky, and both are powerful when the board is already clear.

Here is the contradiction. Every guide tells a new spymaster to go big. Give a 3. Give a 4. Get creative, be clever, stretch the clue. I followed that advice for a whole year and finished under .500. Then I started writing down results, and the pattern was the opposite of what I expected. My winning nights were the boring ones. Small numbers, safe words, and a pile of plain one-word clues late in the game. The number is a lie you tell on purpose. A 4 tells your team you feel great and asks them to gamble four times in a row. A 2 that is obvious wins more games than a 4 that is clever, because the game punishes the second wrong guess, not the first. The best spymasters I know say 2 far more often than 4.

What to Buy, and What to Skip

So now you know how to play. The next question is which box to put on the table.

The base Codenames game is the smart buy for almost everyone. It covers 4 to 8 players out of one $24.97 box, and the full specs live on my Codenames page. Note the number: the base game really wants 4 or more. Two people cannot play it the normal way.

Two variants are worth knowing about. Codenames: Pictures swaps the words for strange little images, which is perfect once your group has memorized the word list, or if your table has kids reading below grade level. It is the same game, about $24.99, and the images are far harder to describe than they look. For exactly two players, Codenames: Duet is the co-op version, about $20, and it turns the whole idea into a puzzle you beat together instead of a fight.

If you want more thinking per turn and a group that plays the same night every week, Decrypto is the deeper sibling. I compared the two head to head in the Codenames vs Decrypto breakdown if you are still choosing. And if someone at your table hates losing, Just One is the friendliest word game of the three, because everyone helps one player instead of fighting.

The Honest Truth About Codenames

Here is the honest truth. The spymaster spends most of the game in silence. You pick one word, then watch four people argue for 90 seconds while you sit there unable to say anything. For an outgoing person, that is a strange seat to be stuck in.

Two more honest notes. The word list repeats. Play with the same four people every week and you will start recognizing cards and reusing the same winning clues, which drains some of the magic. And the assassin can end a night in three minutes. It is rare, but when it happens one person feels awful and the game is over before anyone got going.

The Shelf Test

Here is the Shelf Test. Would this game survive ten plays on a shelf that already holds 40 boxes?

Codenames passes, but only if your table changes. Rotating players, parties, and new crowds keep it fresh forever. The same four people every single week will eventually see the same words twice, and that is when it slows down.

For a two-person shelf, Codenames: Duet is the one to own. It turns the same idea into something you beat together, and it stays tense after twenty plays. That is the box I reach for when it is just me and one other person.

Here is the part that matters. Grab Codenames at about $24.97. It bounces between $20 and $30, so under $25 is a fair deal and under $22 is a grab. Playing with one other person? Take Codenames: Duet instead, around $20. Want images instead of words? Codenames: Pictures is $24.99.
